plot_extraction.response_text:
A naïve but principled young shoe salesman from Oskaloosa moves to Chicago and finds work in a disreputable discount shoe shop. There he meets Sophy Epstein, a pretty, impoverished, streetwise clerk whose only dress is tight, shabby, and cut revealingly low. Although attracted to her, Louie is disturbed by her clothing and by the coarse attention she receives from the other men.

Louie’s respectful treatment unsettles Sophy because it contrasts with the insults and familiarity she normally expects. When he asks her to make her dress more modest, she angrily explains that poverty leaves her too exhausted and ill-equipped to maintain washable, respectable clothes, and that her appearance helps her attract attention and secure meals. Louie sympathizes with her hardship, recounting his own humiliating struggle to wash his clothes while surviving on meager wages, but he still urges her to sew a lace yoke into the dress. She dismisses the suggestion and continues wearing it unchanged.

Soon afterward, Louie encounters an old acquaintance who owns a respectable shoe store and offers him a much better job. Just before Louie is due to leave, Sophy arrives wearing the same dress with a painstakingly assembled black lace yoke covering its low neckline. Mocked by the other clerks, she pretends she altered it only for warmth and fashion. Yet her shy exchange with Louie reveals that his kindness and respect moved her to make the change, while her defiant excuses preserve her pride.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a highly self-conscious, conversational narrative voice that openly comments on the conventions of popular fiction. It begins with an extended comic digression about the supposed obligation to describe a heroine’s clothes, directly addressing the reader through “you” and referring knowingly to writers, publishers, illustrations and stock romantic scenes. This metafictional opening is not merely decorative: it establishes clothing as the story’s governing image and prepares the reader to interpret Sophy’s dress as a sign of poverty, aspiration, vulnerability and social identity. The narrator repeatedly interrupts the action with asides, qualifications and mock explanations, creating the impression of an amused, opinionated storyteller speaking informally to an audience.

The point of view is third-person omniscient, but it is strongly mediated by this intrusive narrator. The narration moves freely between external description, social commentary and glimpses into Louie’s and Sophy’s thoughts. It can summarize an entire social class or urban phenomenon, then narrow its attention to a handkerchief, a washbowl or a scrap of lace. Although the voice frequently jokes at the characters’ expense, it remains sympathetic to them, especially when exposing the pressures created by low wages, exhausting work and the need to maintain appearances. The narrator’s irony is therefore double-edged: it mocks vanity and literary cliché while also revealing the material hardship beneath apparently foolish choices.

The tonal range combines comedy, satire, sentiment and social realism. Much of the humour comes from exaggeration, mock solemnity and incongruous comparisons, as in the treatment of shoe selling as a religion or curiosity as a theatrical force that “plays leads” in life’s dramas. Elevated phrases are often placed beside slang, shabby surroundings or practical worries, producing a comic contrast between romantic language and working-class reality. The story can turn abruptly from flippancy to discomfort or tenderness, particularly in the account of the boss’s unwanted kiss, Louie’s private washing and Sophy’s lunchless sacrifices for jewellery. Its sentiment is carefully protected by wit: emotional moments are usually followed by a joke, a quarrel or a defiant gesture before they can become openly melodramatic.

The diction mixes polished literary narration with period colloquialism, commercial vocabulary, fashion terminology and urban slang. French-derived fashion expressions such as “au fait,” “robe de nuit” and “La Valliere” coexist with “get-up,” “tacky,” “rube,” “fade” and “ferget it.” Brand names, prices, garment details and shoe sizes give the setting material specificity. The language is historically marked by early twentieth-century attitudes and stereotypes, including ethnicized descriptions and broad generalizations about gender and class. Such expressions help locate the piece in its period, though they may strike a modern reader as dated or prejudicial.

Sentence structure is varied and performance-oriented. Long, accumulative sentences are used for comic catalogues, social observation and mounting emphasis, while short sentences deliver punch lines or emotional reversals: “I quit her cold,” “Sophy continued to wear the black dress,” and “Louie did learn.” Parallel constructions and repeated phrasing create rhetorical momentum. The narrator often builds a sequence through anaphora—“He learned … he learned …”—or through escalating alternatives and qualifications. Parentheses, dashes, semicolons, rhetorical questions and direct interjections reproduce the rhythms of spoken storytelling. The prose also uses deliberately formal or grand language to describe ordinary events, turning the contrast itself into humour.

Dialogue is central to characterization and is sharply differentiated from the narrator’s prose. Sophy speaks in compressed, phonetic urban vernacular, with dropped consonants, nonstandard grammar and theatrical slang. Her speech is quick, defensive, mocking and full of verbal feints; humour functions as both social performance and emotional armour. Louie’s language is plainer, more grammatical and more earnest, reflecting his small-town upbringing and moral directness. The boss’s broken syntax and commercial brusqueness establish him immediately as coarse and exploitative. Exchanges frequently operate as contests in which characters negotiate status, attraction and shame. Banter advances the relationship more effectively than explicit declarations would.

Characterization relies on emblematic physical details, social habits and contrasts. Sophy is constructed through paradox: she is “daringly demure,” worldly yet young, brazen in manner yet capable of shame and tenderness. Her revealing black dress initially appears to signify impropriety, but the narrative gradually reframes it as a practical response to poverty and a calculated means of attracting attention in an overcrowded city. Louie is likewise shaped by contrast. He is naïve but professionally knowledgeable, morally conventional but not weak, and comic in his provincial innocence without being treated as contemptible. Their developing attachment is conveyed through changes in behaviour rather than romantic confession, culminating in Sophy’s decision to sew in the lace yoke.

The structure is circular and symbolically concentrated. The opening discussion of costume leads into a detailed account of Sophy’s dress; the central conflict repeatedly returns to its low-cut V; and the conclusion transforms that same garment through the makeshift yoke. This gives the story a clear progression from appearance, through dispute and mutual recognition, to a modest act of change. The ending remains indirect. Sophy refuses to admit that Louie influenced her and invents practical and fashionable excuses, while her defiance preserves her pride. The emotional resolution lies in the discrepancy between what she says and what the reader knows.

Imagery is predominantly concrete and urban. Shop windows, elevators, display cases, mosaic floors, cramped rooms, cheap jewellery and piles of shoes create a commercial city organized around display and exchange. Clothes and footwear function as an extended social metaphor: they reveal class, aspiration and employability, but they can also disguise need. The shoe shop is especially effective as a setting because it joins appearance to deception; inferior goods are made to look valuable just as workers must market themselves through dress, charm and performance. References to the stage, actors, balconies and “stage managers” reinforce the idea that city life requires continuous self-presentation.

The story’s thematic style depends on exposing the economic realities hidden beneath judgments about taste and morality. It examines the conflict between provincial standards and urban survival, the vulnerability of working women, the humiliations of male and female poverty, and the emotional significance of courtesy. Louie initially treats Sophy’s dress as a moral failing, while Sophy forces him to understand its practical purpose. In turn, his respectful treatment awakens in her a nearly forgotten desire to be regarded differently. The narrative does not wholly endorse either character’s position; instead, it lets their argument reveal how poverty complicates respectability.

Overall, the style is witty, intrusive, socially observant and emotionally warm. Its defining qualities are direct reader address, comic digression, ironic contrast, vivid material detail, dialect-heavy dialogue and a recurring symbolic object. The prose moves between caricature and compassion, using humour to make social criticism palatable and withholding overt romance in favour of gesture, implication and a final defensive joke.

generation.response_text:
The publishers have a rule—whether printed in black ink and nailed above the editorial desk, or merely communicated by the lifting of an eyebrow—that a heroine must not enter a story improperly dressed.

I do not mean improperly in the moral sense. Morality is permitted to arrive late, after the second installment, and sometimes does not arrive at all. I mean that the reader must be told what the heroine has on. You may introduce a young man with nothing more than a name and an appetite. You may say, “Henry came in,” and Henry is accepted, hat, trousers, collar, and all. But if you write, “Marcella entered,” somebody immediately demands to know whether she wore blue voile, white organdie, biscuit-colored broadcloth, or one of those simple little frocks whose simplicity costs eighty-seven dollars.

The illustrator demands it first. How can he draw Marcella if you leave her suspended in the atmosphere like a disembodied virtue? The publisher demands it next, because women buy magazines and women, according to publishers, study the heroine’s sleeves before consenting to feel anxiety about her soul. Finally you demand it yourself. Do not deny this. If Marcella steps onto a moonlit balcony, you want to know whether the moon shines on chiffon or satin.

Therefore Sophy Epstein must be described by her dress.

This is unfortunate, because Sophy had only one.

It was black, or had once been black, and it fitted her with an accuracy not wholly attributable to the dressmaker. There had been no dressmaker. Sophy and a girl named Tillie Rosen had cut it from a paper pattern upon the kitchen table in Mrs. Epstein’s flat, where the gravy stains on the oilcloth gave several of the pieces an adventurous bias. It was tight at the waist, tighter at the hips, short enough to display two narrow ankles, and cut in front to a V of such daring depth that every man in Klein’s Cut-Rate Shoe Emporium became, on beholding it, a student of geometry.

The dress had other qualities. It did not show dirt. It could be worn to work, to a dance hall, to a funeral, or—if Sophy ever found time for one—to church. A ribbon altered its politics. A string of glass beads raised its social standing. A spot of powder on the shoulders prepared it for evening.

It was, in short, a highly efficient dress.

Louie Baer disliked it immediately.

Louie had come from Oskaloosa, Iowa, where dresses knew their place and remained there. They rose to the throat, descended to the shoe tops, and gave no information not demanded by law. In Oskaloosa Louie had sold footwear for Mr. T. E. Bixby, who kept a walnut ruler under the counter, attended the Methodist church, and considered the fitting of a shoe a sacred trust.

Louie believed likewise. A customer might lie about her age, her weight, her husband’s salary, and the natural color of her hair; but when she said she wore a four-B, Louie’s face became grave. Feet were facts. He would kneel, measure, test the arch, and say, “Madam, you require a five-C,” with the calm bravery of a physician announcing appendicitis.

Chicago received him without enthusiasm.

Chicago receives five thousand young men every week who have been assured at home that the city is waiting for them. The city is generally looking the other way.

For nine days Louie called upon shoe houses from State Street to the river, carrying letters which said he was sober, industrious, honest, and acquainted with the McKay stitch. Honesty was not then in brisk demand. Neither was the McKay stitch. On the tenth morning his landlady informed him that the room rent was due; on the tenth afternoon he entered Klein’s Cut-Rate Shoe Emporium and accepted nine dollars a week.

Klein’s occupied a long, narrow room beneath an elevated railway. Every three minutes a train passed overhead and shook dust into the children’s shoes. The front window contained twenty-seven pairs of ladies’ footwear, each resting upon crimson plush and each marked with a price ending in ninety-eight cents. Nothing in the store had ever cost a round sum. Klein believed that humanity would resist two dollars to the death but surrender instantly to one dollar and ninety-eight cents.

The shoes were equally diplomatic. Pasteboard soles masqueraded as leather. Heels concealed private weaknesses. Patent-leather pumps shone with the desperate brilliance of people who know they will not last.

Mr. Klein himself was a broad, pale man with diamonds on two fingers and a permanent dampness about the lips.

“You sell quick,” he told Louie. “No sermons. Lady says five, give four-and-a-half if it don’t hurt too loud. Everything genuine. Understand?”

“No, sir,” said Louie.

Klein stared.

“I mean—yes, sir.”

Thus Louie entered metropolitan commerce.

He learned many things. He learned that a shoe could be “Parisian” without ever having left Milwaukee. He learned that a woman who could scarcely walk in a pump would buy it if told that her foot looked two sizes smaller. He learned that the proper answer to “Is this real calf?” was not necessarily the answer taught in Oskaloosa. He learned to say “special line,” “factory surplus,” and “just your style.”

He did not learn to lie well. His ears reddened before the falsehood emerged, thereby making it useless except to customers of defective eyesight.

Sophy Epstein worked at the ribbon counter near the rear, though “ribbon counter” gives too festive an impression. There were shoestrings, buckles, polish, insoles, hose, and three cards of pink ribbon left from a season when pink ribbon had briefly threatened to become essential to civilization. Sophy sold all these, wrapped parcels, answered the telephone, carried stock, soothed angry customers, and, when Mr. Klein’s bookkeeper failed to appear, added columns of figures. For this she received seven dollars.

She was nineteen, small and thin, with cloudy dark hair, gray eyes, and a mouth that seemed always to have heard the beginning of a joke. Her beauty was not the restful sort. It flashed, contradicted itself, challenged you, and then withdrew. One minute she looked like a child who ought to be given a bowl of soup; the next, like a young woman who had already learned that bowls of soup are seldom given without questions.

The men in the store called her Soph, Baby, Queenie, Toots, and several other names not bestowed at baptism.

“Say, Soph,” cried Gus, the window trimmer, on Louie’s first day, “ain’t you cold in that ballroom wrapper?”

“Cold?” said Sophy. “With you around? You’re a human furnace, Gus—mostly smoke.”

The clerks laughed.

When she bent to lift a carton, Benny Loeb whistled. Sophy straightened slowly.

“You practising to call dogs, Benny?”

“Only the good-lookin’ ones.”

“Then whistle in a mirror.”

She could defend herself. Indeed, she defended herself so continuously that the defense had become part of her manner, like the bangles on her wrist. Yet Louie noticed that after the laughter she sometimes turned away quickly. He noticed, too, how Klein brushed against her when passing in the narrow aisle, though there was room enough for a piano.

One evening Klein called her into the stockroom.

Louie, sorting misses’ button boots outside, heard Klein say, “Come on, Sophy. Don’t be so high-toned.”

Then came the scrape of a box, a sharp slap, and Sophy’s voice:

“You try that again and I’ll feed you them patent leathers—buckles first.”

She came out with one cheek crimson. Seeing Louie, she stopped. Her hand went at once to the low V of her dress—not covering it, precisely, but touching it as if she had suddenly remembered it was there.

Louie looked down at the boots.

Sophy waited for a grin, a wink, or a question. Men’s curiosity, she had found, was an actor who could play every part from friend to magistrate. But Louie only said, “That six is in the five-and-a-half box.”

“What?”

“This boot. It’s marked wrong.”

“Oh.”

She returned to her counter. For the rest of the evening she was unusually silent, which disturbed everybody and caused Gus to ask whether she had swallowed a shoehorn.

Louie’s courtesy troubled her more than the insults. An insult could be struck back. Courtesy left no convenient handle.

The next day he said, “Good morning, Miss Epstein.”

She looked behind her.

“Who you talkin’ to?”

“You.”

“Then cut out the Miss. Makes me feel like I’m forty and own a parrot.”

“All right—Sophy.”

“That’s better, Iowa.”

She had named him Iowa before learning his surname, and the name stuck. She mocked his careful speech, his shiny Sunday tie, and his habit of saying “Excuse me” to customers who stepped on him. But when a woman complained that Sophy had short-changed her, Louie quietly produced the sales slip and proved otherwise. When Benny hid a dead beetle in her cash drawer, Louie removed it before she opened the drawer. When Klein asked her to stay late for “inventory,” Louie announced that he, too, would remain.

Klein discovered that the inventory could wait.

This went on for three weeks. Nothing in the behavior would have interested a motion-picture director. There were no moonlit balconies. There was one alley behind the store, but it smelled of cabbage and contained a cat of violent politics. Nevertheless, Louie began to think about Sophy while brushing his teeth, which is one of the least romantic yet most reliable signs of affection.

He admired her quickness. He pitied her thin wrists. He disliked her slang, her powder, her cheap bangles, the company she kept, and most particularly the dress.

One Saturday the store remained open until eleven. Near ten, trade slackened. Gus and Benny went to the corner for coffee. Klein was arguing by telephone with a wholesaler who wished to be paid. Sophy sat on a stool, rubbing one foot.

Louie approached her.

“Does it hurt?”

“Naw. I’m rubbin’ it for luck.”

“You ought to wear a wider shoe.”

“Listen to Professor Foot.”

“You’re in a three-A. You need a four-B.”

“I need four bucks. The B can stand for breakfast.”

Louie smiled, then became serious. Seriousness came upon him with no warning and sat heavily.

“Sophy, may I say something?”

“You usually do.”

“I wish you wouldn’t wear that dress so—so open.”

Her hand ceased rubbing the foot.

“What’s it to you?”

“I don’t like the way those fellows look at you.”

“They got eyes. Want me to collect ’em in a cup?”

“They don’t show you respect.”

At that word her face changed. A shutter came down behind the gray eyes.

“Respect! Say, Iowa, did you buy a job lot of respect before you left the farm?”

“I’m not trying to insult you.”

“You’re doin’ swell without tryin’.”

“I only mean you could put something in there. A piece of lace. A yoke, maybe.”

“A yoke!” Sophy laughed. It was not her regular laugh. This one had edges. “Hear him! Go get me a yoke, Gus—white lace, handmade by starving duchesses.”

“I didn’t say white.”

“No, black. Black’s refined. Black takes me right into society.”

“Sophy—”

She sprang from the stool.

“You think I like wearin’ this rag every day? You think I don’t know it’s shiny under the arms and split under the belt? What d’you suppose I do nights—sit in a limousine and fan myself?”

“I never said—”

“I get home after twelve Saturdays. There’s Ma coughin’, two kids in one bed, and the sink piled to the ceiling. We got one iron, and you got to heat it on the stove. Coal costs money. Soap costs money. Hot water’s a celebration. If I wear a white waist, it’s dirty Tuesday. Then what? Come Wednesday in a barrel?”

Louie stood very still.

Sophy’s voice dropped, but its bitterness increased.

“This dress don’t show dirt. I brush it. I sponge the spots with benzine. I sew it when it busts. It’s the only thing I got that don’t look like I came out of a rag bag.”

“You might have it cut higher.”

“Sure. I’ll ask the dressmaker I keep in the linen closet.”

“You and your friend made it, didn’t you?”

“Tillie’s workin’ nights now. Anyway, there ain’t cloth.”

“A little lace wouldn’t cost much.”

“A little lace wouldn’t cost much,” she mimicked. “Seven dollars a week don’t cost much either, if you ain’t buyin’ food.”

Louie flushed. He had thought himself poor. Sophy was showing him that poverty has grades, departments, and postgraduate courses.

She touched the beads at her throat—a glittering string of imitation jet.

“You think these are foolish too, don’t you?”

“I didn’t say so.”

“You looked it. They cost thirty-nine cents. I skipped lunch twice. That’s foolish, huh?”

“Yes,” said Louie honestly.

“Well, maybe it is. But when I put ’em on, people see the beads before they see the dress is old. A girl’s got to look like somebody in this town. If she looks hungry, everybody lets her stay hungry.”

Louie had no reply.

Sophy went on, because once pride begins confessing its injuries it must talk fast or stop altogether.

“And if a fellow likes the look of me and takes me to supper, what’s the crime? I ain’t askin’ him to buy the restaurant. A chop’s a chop. You can eat respect when they put gravy on it.”

“I’d take you to supper.”

“That ain’t the point.”

“Why not?”

“Because you’d sit there lookin’ like I was your Sunday-school class.”

The elevated train roared overhead. A tower of shoe boxes trembled. One fell, struck the floor, and burst open, revealing a pair of bronze slippers of extraordinary ugliness.

Louie picked them up.

“When I first came here,” he said, “I had two shirts.”

Sophy folded her arms.

“Congratulations.”

“I washed one every night in the bowl at my room. The bowl was about this big.” He made a circle with his hands. “The landlady wouldn’t give me hot water. I scrubbed the collar with shaving soap and hung the shirt over the bed.”

Sophy’s mouth twitched.

“One morning it was still wet, so I put it on wet. It dried on me while I walked to State Street.”

“That why you’re shaped so funny?”

“Probably.”

She almost smiled.

“I wore the cuffs until the edges frayed. I trimmed them with scissors, but one got crooked. A manager saw it when I applied for work. He kept looking at that cuff while I told him I knew fitting, stock numbers, and children’s corrective shoes. He said they had no opening.”

Louie turned the bronze slipper in his hands.

“I wanted to tell him I was clean. The cuff was clean. It was only worn out. But saying that would have made it worse.”

Sophy’s arms loosened.

“Yeah,” she said. “It always makes it worse.”

For a moment they possessed that rarest of luxuries—complete understanding. Naturally, neither knew what to do with it.

Louie put the slippers back in their box.

“Still,” he said, “I wish you’d put in the lace.”

Sophy stared at him.

Then she snatched the box from his hands and shoved it onto the shelf.

“Still! You pig-headed cornfield! I tell you the whole story of my life, with orchestra accompaniment, and you come back with lace!”

“I don’t mean—”

“Ferget it.”

“Sophy—”

“I said ferget it. Go sell a shoe.”

She marched to her counter. The conversation was concluded with all diplomatic relations severed.

On Monday Sophy wore the black dress unchanged.

On Tuesday she wore it unchanged.

Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday found the V still pursuing its reckless journey. If Louie glanced at it, Sophy caught him and smiled sweetly.

“Nice cool weather, ain’t it, Iowa?”

He never mentioned lace again.

Their acquaintance, however, survived. Poverty makes quarrels expensive; persons who work ten feet apart cannot afford the luxury of eternal estrangement. Sophy resumed teasing him. Louie resumed protecting her without admitting that he did so. He brought an apple for lunch one day and discovered, after waiting until four, that he was not hungry and Sophy was. She ate it without thanking him, which was her way of accepting the delicacy of the transaction.

She taught him Chicago.

She taught him never to buy a newspaper from the boy with the bandaged arm, because the bandage moved from arm to arm according to fatigue. She taught him that a restaurant advertising “home cooking” usually had a cook who had left home under painful circumstances. She showed him where coffee was five cents, where neckties were reduced after six, and which elevated guard would hold the door for a girl running upstairs.

He taught her shoes.

He taught her that a high instep could make a cheap pump torture, that children’s feet ought not be forced into sizes left over from last season, and that when a tired woman said, “Anything comfortable,” she was to be believed instead of sold the pair with the largest commission.

“Shoes is your religion, ain’t they?” Sophy asked.

“They’re important.”

“Sure. Souls can go barefoot, but feet got to be saved.”

Even Mr. Klein noticed Louie’s ability. Customers returned and asked for him. This annoyed Klein, who preferred customers to return only after their purchases had become too worn to exchange.

Then, one rainy afternoon, a stout man with a reddish mustache entered the store. His umbrella dripped upon Klein’s mosaic floor—a floor so called because three colors of linoleum had been patched into it.

“Louie Baer!” he exclaimed.

Louie looked up from a pair of button shoes.

“Mr. Hanford!”

The man was Elias Hanford, formerly of Oskaloosa and now proprietor of Hanford’s Family Shoe Store on North Clark Street. His shop had polished oak fittings, honest leather, and a mechanical rocking horse for children. He had come to Klein’s because the rain had driven him beneath the awning, but Providence often works under awnings.

They talked. Mr. Hanford asked questions. Louie answered. Klein hovered, moist and suspicious.

That evening Hanford took Louie to dinner and offered him fifteen dollars a week, with an increase to eighteen if he proved satisfactory.

Fifteen dollars! Respectable stock! Regular closing at six except Saturdays! No pasteboard announced as calf!

Louie accepted.

He was to begin Monday.

On Friday he told Sophy.

She was arranging boxes of shoe polish.

“Hanford’s?” she said. “That swell joint with the wood horse?”

“Yes.”

“Fifteen a week?”

“Yes.”

“Gee. You’ll be wearin’ spats.”

“I don’t think so.”

“Don’t forget us lowlifes when you’re president of the shoe trust.”

“I won’t forget you.”

Sophy dropped a tin. It rolled beneath the counter.

“Who asked you to remember?”

“Nobody.”

“Then don’t get mushy.”

“I wasn’t.”

“You had the symptoms.”

She knelt to retrieve the tin and remained hidden longer than necessary. When she rose, her grin was in place.

“Better watch Hanford. Respectable stores is dangerous. First thing you know, you’ll marry a lady customer with a bunion and a bank account.”

Louie wanted to say something. He did not know what. A declaration would have been premature, presumptuous, and impossible at nine dollars a week. At fifteen it became only premature and presumptuous.

“I may come back,” he said.

“What for? Our shoes?”

“To see everybody.”

“Everybody’ll be thrilled.”

Saturday was his last day.

At nine-thirty Sophy had not appeared. This was unusual. Klein complained, Benny suggested that she had eloped with a millionaire, and Gus offered odds that the millionaire would return her before lunch.

Louie said nothing. He sold shoes. He sold a pair of gray pumps to a woman who wanted brown, and when she returned them ten minutes later, he apologized so earnestly that she bought the brown pair as well. Such is the commercial value of misery when properly directed.

At eleven the door opened and Sophy entered.

She was breathless, her cheeks pink from the wind. She wore the black dress.

But across its deep V, from shoulder to shoulder and throat to breast, there now extended a yoke of black lace.

It was not the lace of duchesses. No starving noblewoman had blinded herself over it in a Belgian tower. It consisted, if truth must invade the scene, of three separate remnants skillfully persuaded to look acquainted. One piece bore roses, another spiderwebs, and the third a design suggesting damaged cabbages. The seams had been joined with tiny, painful stitches. At the throat a narrow strip of black ribbon concealed a place where the supply had failed.

It was cheap. It was uneven. It was beautiful.

Sophy marched behind her counter as if nothing had occurred.

The store became silent.

Gus recovered first.

“Holy smoke! Soph’s put a fence around the property.”

Benny leaned across a display case.

“What’s the matter, kid? Reform wave hit town?”

Sophy removed her hat.

“Reform nothin’. It’s cold.”

“Cold? It’s sixty-two.”

“My neck’s delicate.”

Klein emerged from the stockroom and surveyed the alteration with disfavor. The dress had been, in his opinion, an asset to trade.

“Vat’s this funeral curtain?”

Sophy smiled brilliantly.

“This? Latest thing. All the swell dames is wearin’ ’em. La Valliere neck effect. You wouldn’t know, Mr. Klein. It’s French.”

Klein distrusted France but feared appearing ignorant of it.

“Looks cheap,” he muttered.

“Cost enough.”

“How much?” Benny asked.

“None of your business.”

“Bet she made it.”

“Bet I didn’t.”

“You did too. Look at them stitches.”

“They come from Paris that way, rube.”

The clerks laughed. Sophy laughed louder. Only Louie, at the fitting stool, did not laugh.

He saw the lace. He saw also the needle puncture on her left forefinger, the faint blue shadows under her eyes, and a loose thread near the ribbon where, in haste, she had failed to knot it. He imagined the kitchen after midnight: the coughing mother, the sleeping children, the smoking lamp, the scraps spread upon stained oilcloth. He imagined Sophy bending over them, swearing when the thread broke, perhaps throwing the whole thing down, perhaps picking it up again.

The reader may imagine these things too. That is one privilege the reader possesses over the characters. Louie could not ask. Sophy would have denied every stitch.

At noon he found her alone beside the stock shelves.

“It looks nice,” he said.

“What does?”

“The lace.”

“Oh, that.” She examined a polish tin. “I told ’em. My neck gets cold.”

“Yes.”

“And it’s stylish.”

“Yes.”

“All the girls’ll be wearin’ ’em.”

“I expect so.”

She glanced at him suspiciously.

“If you think I done it on account of what you said—”

“I didn’t say that.”

“Because I didn’t.”

“All right.”

“I’d been plannin’ it for months.”

“Of course.”

“Tillie give me the scraps. I hadda use ’em or throw ’em out.”

“That was sensible.”

She set down the tin with violence.

“Don’t stand there agreein’ with me!”

“I’m sorry.”

“And quit lookin’ at me like that.”

“How am I looking?”

“Like—like a shoe clerk in a stained-glass window.”

Louie smiled.

Sophy’s defiance faltered. For one second she looked nineteen—not streetwise, not daring, not equipped with jokes and beads and a dress that did the work of three dresses, but simply nineteen and uncertain.

“Honest?” she asked.

“Honest what?”

“It looks all right?”

“It looks very nice.”

“Not tacky?”

“No.”

“Gus says the middle piece don’t match.”

“Gus wears purple socks.”

“That’s true.”

She touched the ribbon at her throat. Her fingers trembled once and became still.

“You’ll be in tomorrow to get your pay?”

“Yes.”

“I won’t be here. Ma’s takin’ bad. I’m stayin’ home.”

“I’m sorry.”

“She ain’t dyin’. She just likes attention.”

“I’ll come by sometime.”

“To the flat?”

“If you don’t mind.”

Sophy’s gray eyes met his.

“Bring fruit,” she said. “Not flowers. Flowers is no good to eat.”

“I’ll bring fruit.”

“And don’t wear spats.”

“I won’t.”

“And don’t think this lace means anything.”

“I don’t.”

“It don’t.”

“I understand.”

“You don’t understand nothin’, Iowa.”

“Maybe not.”

She turned away, but not before he saw her smile.

At six o’clock Louie left Klein’s Cut-Rate Shoe Emporium. Mr. Klein shook his hand and said he could return at the old wage if Hanford discharged him. Gus gave him a cigar of criminal manufacture. Benny borrowed a quarter.

Sophy remained behind her counter, although her mother, it appeared, had postponed taking bad until Sunday.

Louie paused at the door.

“Good night, Sophy.”

“Good night, Mr. Baer.”

It was the first time she had called him that.

The elevated train thundered overhead. Dust descended. The window shoes trembled upon their crimson plush, displaying their false soles, their weak heels, and their little white cards proclaiming impossible bargains. Outside, Chicago shoved and shouted beneath the lamps. Everybody was selling something—shoes, ribbons, labor, beauty, honesty, or the appearance of having eaten lunch.

Louie stepped into the crowd.

Behind him Sophy adjusted the black lace yoke. Then, discovering Benny watching, she scowled.

“Whatcha starin’ at?”

“Nothin’.”

“Well, keep on starin’ at it.”

And she lifted her chin, now modestly, stubbornly, splendidly covered to the throat.

## The House That Waited for Rain

In Bellweather, rain had not fallen for twenty-two years.

Children learned about it from picture books: silver lines slanting across windows, umbrellas blooming along city streets, puddles holding pieces of the sky. Their parents spoke of rain the way people spoke of vanished animals or distant wars. They remembered its smell, they said. They remembered the drumming on rooftops, the rivers climbing their banks, the impatient squelch of mud beneath boots.

But Bellweather’s children had never heard thunder.

Every morning, the town’s water train arrived from the northern reservoirs. It came shrieking across the salt flats, dragging twelve iron tanks behind it. By noon, each family had collected its weekly measure. By evening, the empty train was gone, and the horizon lay bare again.

Mara Venn maintained the town’s clocks.

There were sixty-three public clocks in Bellweather: one in the railway station, four in the school, seven in the abandoned factory, and fifty-one scattered among shops, offices, and civic buildings. Most were unnecessary. Everyone carried a government-issued watch, synchronized daily by radio. Yet the mayor insisted the old clocks continue running.

“A town without clocks,” he often said, “is a town waiting to disappear.”

Mara understood waiting better than most. Twelve years earlier, her father had walked south to repair a weather station and never returned. Search parties found his truck, his tools, and one boot beside a dry ravine. No body. No note.

Her mother had waited at the front window every evening until illness took her. Mara waited differently. She repaired clocks, counted train cars, and never looked south unless work required it.

One August morning, while servicing the clock in the railway station, Mara found an envelope inside the case.

It lay behind the pendulum, sealed with blue wax. Her name was written across the front in handwriting she recognized immediately.

MARA VENN.

The screwdriver slipped from her fingers and struck the floor.

She stared at the envelope while the clock ticked around her.

Her father’s handwriting had been narrow and slightly tilted, as if each word were leaning into a strong wind. She remembered seeing it on grocery lists and birthday cards, on labels tied to jars of screws. She had not seen it in twelve years.

Mara broke the seal.

Inside was a single sheet of paper.

_When the station clock stops at 4:17, go to the house beyond the southern ridge. Bring the brass key from my workshop. Do not let anyone follow you._

_Before the rain comes, you must open the door._

The letter was signed:

_Dad._

Mara read it three times.

Then the station clock stopped.

The minute hand rested at seventeen minutes past four, though the morning was barely nine.

Behind her, the stationmaster cleared his throat.

“Problem?”

Mara folded the letter into her pocket. “Broken mainspring.”

“Can you fix it?”

“Not today.”

This was a lie. Mara could have replaced the mainspring in twenty minutes. Instead, she packed her tools and bicycled home beneath a white, merciless sun.

Her father’s workshop stood behind the house. Mara had kept it locked since her mother’s death. Dust softened every surface: the workbench, the metal cabinets, the shelves crowded with instruments. A cracked barometer hung beside the door, its needle pointing forever toward STORM.

She found the brass key in the bottom drawer of his desk.

It was longer than her hand, green with age, and tied to a wooden tag. On the tag, her father had carved a small cloud.

Mara almost returned it to the drawer.

The letter could not be recent. Someone might have found an old note and placed it in the station clock as a cruel joke. Yet only Mara knew where the key was. Only her father had known how deeply she loved opening clock cases and discovering messages he had hidden inside.

When she was nine, he had tucked a note into the kitchen clock.

_Look beneath the blue flowerpot._

Beneath it, she had found a paper bird.

The next note led her to the well, the next to the school bell, the next to the railway signal. At the end of the trail, her father waited on the roof with a telescope aimed at a passing comet.

“Some things only appear if you know where and when to look,” he had told her.

Mara slipped the brass key into her bag.

By sunset, she was walking south.

Beyond Bellweather, the land rose into low, stony ridges. No road crossed them. Mara followed a cattle path erased in places by dust. Heat lingered after dark, radiating from the ground. Above her, the stars were painfully bright.

She walked for three hours before finding the house.

It stood alone in a hollow, half buried by drifting sand. Two stories tall, it had narrow windows, a steep roof, and a porch that sagged beneath the weight of emptiness. A weather vane shaped like a swallow turned slowly overhead, though there was no wind.

Mara had seen no house marked on any map.

As she approached, a light appeared behind an upstairs window.

She stopped.

A shadow moved across the curtain.

“Hello?” she called.

The front door opened.

A boy of about fifteen stood inside, holding an oil lamp. His clothes were old-fashioned: patched trousers, collarless shirt, suspenders. His hair was dark and badly cut.

“You’re late,” he said.

Mara gripped the brass key inside her bag. “Who are you?”

“Elias.”

“Do you live here?”

“Not exactly.”

“Is my father here?”

The boy studied her face. “You look like him.”

Mara stepped onto the porch. “Where is he?”

Elias retreated into the hall. “You should come in. The night gets dangerous when the house is awake.”

“The house?”

The front door swung shut behind Mara.

Inside, the air was cool and smelled of cedar, dust, and something else—something so familiar that her chest tightened.

Wet earth.

The hall contained dozens of clocks. Grandfather clocks, carriage clocks, brass marine chronometers, tiny silver watches beneath glass domes. None showed the same time. Their ticking filled the house like restless insects.

At the end of the corridor stood a black door without a handle.

Mara drew out the key.

Elias’s eyes widened. “He gave it to you.”

“He left it for me.”

“That’s different.”

“Where is my father?”

The boy placed his lamp on a table. “There are rules. The house can preserve what enters it, but it cannot always preserve things in the right order.”

“I don’t want riddles.”

“They aren’t riddles.” Elias glanced at the clocks. “What year is it?”

“Year 82 of the Republic.”

His face went pale.

“What?”

“When I came here, it was Year 59.”

Mara looked him over again. “You expect me to believe you’ve been here twenty-three years?”

“For me, it’s been six months.”

A clock chimed once. Another answered with seven uneven notes.

Elias lowered his voice. “The house was built by Ada Wren, before the Republic, when Bellweather was still called Mercy Ford. She studied storms. She believed time and weather were the same thing in different forms.”

“That makes no sense.”

“She said a clock measures change, not time. Weather does the same. A cloud changes into rain. Water changes into rivers. Rivers change stone. Stop change, and you can stop all of it.”

Mara thought of the town, dry and unchanging beneath its white sky.

Elias pointed to the black door. “Ada built a machine below the house. When the Great Drought began, people begged her to stop the sky from losing its last storm. So she caught it.”

“Caught what?”

“The rain.”

The smell of wet earth seemed stronger now.

Elias continued. “She trapped the storm inside a single moment. It saved the valley from flooding, but the moment never ended. The storm can’t move forward, and neither can the weather outside. That’s why it hasn’t rained.”

Mara stared at the black door. “And my father?”

“He found the house twelve years ago. He tried to release the storm.”

“Where is he?”

“On the other side.”

Mara pushed the brass key into the lock.

Elias seized her wrist. “Wait. The room below doesn’t follow ordinary time. If you open the door at the wrong moment, the storm could be released all at once. Twenty-two years of rain in a few seconds.”

“Then tell me the right moment.”

“I don’t know.”

“My father’s letter said before the rain comes.”

“The rain is always coming. It simply never arrives.”

Mara turned the key.

The black door opened onto a staircase descending into blue light.

At its foot was a vast underground chamber.

A machine filled the room. Copper pipes coiled around glass cylinders. Silver wheels spun without touching one another. Pendulums swung in impossible directions. In the center stood a sphere of clear crystal, taller than a person.

Inside the sphere hung a raindrop.

It trembled in empty air.

Mara approached it slowly. Within the drop she saw a gray sky, fields bending beneath wind, and rain falling across a greener Bellweather. The image shifted. Lightning split the horizon. Water poured through streets. People ran laughing from doorways.

Then she saw her father.

He was standing in the rain, looking directly at her.

Mara lifted a hand to the crystal.

Her father mirrored her movement.

His lips formed her name.

“Dad?”

The machinery shuddered.

Every pendulum stopped.

Elias shouted from the stairs. “Don’t touch it!”

A spark jumped between Mara’s fingers and the sphere.

The chamber vanished.

She stood in Bellweather’s main square beneath a dark, churning sky.

Rain struck her face.

For a moment, she could do nothing but feel it. Cold drops touched her eyelids, lips, and hands. They soaked her hair and ran beneath her collar. The scent of wet dust rose around her, rich and almost sweet.

Across the square, a man stood beside the dry fountain.

Her father had not aged.

He wore the same sun-bleached jacket from the day he disappeared. His hair was black, his face lean. A coil of rope hung from one shoulder.

“Mara,” he said.

She crossed the square at a run.

He caught her, and she buried her face against his chest. His arms tightened around her with desperate strength.

“You’re grown,” he whispered.

She tried to answer, but twelve years of grief had become something larger than words.

At last she stepped back. “Where have you been?”

“Here. In the last minute before the storm was trapped.” He looked around the empty square. “I thought it had been an hour, perhaps two.”

“You wrote me a letter.”

“I haven’t yet.”

Mara took it from her pocket.

He read the note, and she watched understanding move across his face.

“The house must have carried it backward after I wrote it.”

“You knew I’d come.”

“I hoped.” He returned the letter. “I’m sorry.”

Anger flared through her. “You’re sorry? Mother waited for you until she died.”

His face collapsed.

Mara regretted the words but did not take them back.

“She’s gone?” he asked.

“Three years ago.”

The rain passed through him strangely, droplets slowing as they touched his jacket.

“I thought I could fix it,” he said. “The drought, the machine, all of it. I thought I would be home by supper.”

“You always thought you could repair everything.”

“Yes.” He looked toward the clock tower. Its hands showed 4:16. “And I was often wrong.”

Thunder rolled across the town.

Mara turned. At the far end of the square, a wall of water hung above the rooftops, frozen in the act of crashing down.

“The storm Ada trapped caused a flood,” her father said. “She stopped time to save the town. But the machine has weakened. Soon the moment will break on its own.”

“How soon?”

“The station clock marks the strain. When it reaches 4:17, the machine fails.”

“It already reached 4:17 in my time.”

“Then there isn’t long.”

“How do we release the rain safely?”

Her father pointed to the clock tower. “The machine needs a regulator—one clock connected to both moments. I tried to use the station clock, but I couldn’t reach its mechanism from here.”

“I can.”

“I know.”

The square flickered. For an instant, Mara saw dusty streets beneath blazing sun. Then rain and darkness returned.

“What must I do?”

“Restart the station clock and set it to the true time. When it begins moving, the trapped minute will move with it. The storm will unfold over hours instead of seconds.”

“Then come with me.”

He shook his head.

“No.”

“I’m part of the trapped moment now.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I do.”

“Then I’ll find another way.”

“Mara.” He put both hands on her shoulders. “Some things cannot be repaired without changing them.”

The square flickered again. Elias appeared near the fountain, translucent as smoke.

“Hurry!” he called. “The house is coming apart!”

The station clock began to strike.

One.

The frozen wall of water moved.

Two.

Her father pulled the coil of rope from his shoulder. On its end was a small metal gear.

“This belongs in the station clock. I removed it twelve years ago, trying to stop the mechanism from failing.”

“Taking it caused the clock to stop.”

“Taking it allowed the clock to send the letter. Cause and consequence aren’t behaving politely.”

Three.

He pressed the gear into her palm.

She closed her fingers around it. “Come back with me.”

“I can’t.”

“Try.”

He smiled then, and she saw the man who had hidden paper birds beneath flowerpots.

Four.

Elias grabbed her hand. The square stretched around them, buildings bending like reflections in disturbed water.

Mara held tightly to her father.

For one impossible second, all three stood together between drought and storm.

Then her father’s fingers slipped through hers.

The underground chamber returned.

Gears screamed. Copper pipes burst from the walls. Cracks spread across the crystal sphere, and water leaked through them, floating upward in shining beads.

Elias dragged Mara toward the stairs.

They reached the hall as the black door slammed behind them. Every clock in the house was striking now, their bells colliding in a roar.

The front door opened onto the railway station.

Not the southern ridge. Not the desert. The station.

Mara stumbled across the platform. Outside, Bellweather slept beneath the stars.

The clock above the ticket office showed 4:17.

She ran to it, pulled a bench beneath the case, and climbed. Her hands shook as she opened the glass.

The missing gear left a dark space in the mechanism.

Mara fitted the gear onto its post.

Nothing happened.

“What’s wrong?” Elias asked.

“The mainspring has no tension.”

“Can you fix it?”

“Yes.”

She inserted the winding key and turned.

Once.

Twice.

Outside, lightning flashed.

On the third turn, the key kicked backward and sliced her palm.

A low sound passed over the town.

Thunder.

Lights appeared in windows. Doors opened. People stepped into the streets wearing nightclothes, staring upward.

Mara wound the spring again.

The clock ticked.

The minute hand shivered, moved backward to 4:16, and began its journey forward.

A drop of rain struck the station window.

Then another.

Mara climbed down and walked outside.

All across Bellweather, people stood in silence. No one ran for shelter. No one opened an umbrella. Faces tilted toward the sky as rain began to fall.

It came gently.

Children laughed first. They reached up, trying to catch the drops. Adults followed, some shouting, some weeping. Mayor Vale emerged from his house in a red robe and fell to his knees in the mud.

The rain touched everything: roofs, roads, dust, gardens, railway tracks. It rang against the water tanks and washed twenty-two years of salt from the station walls.

Elias stood beneath the awning.

“You can come out,” Mara told him.

He watched the rain nervously. “I’ve never seen it.”

“Neither have I.”

“That’s not true.”

Mara remembered the trapped square, her father’s arms, the cold drops passing between them.

“Not like this,” she said.

Elias stepped into the rain.

At once, he began to change. His body stretched. His face sharpened. His patched clothes shifted into a dark uniform, then a laborer’s coat, then a suit. Years moved over him like shadows of clouds.

When the change ended, a gray-haired man stood before her.

He looked at his hands. “It seems time remembered me.”

“Are you all right?”

“I don’t know yet.”

The rain fell for seven hours.

It filled gutters and barrels, darkened the hills, and woke seeds that had waited beneath the earth for decades. It softened the hard bed of the river. It ran through the cemetery, where Mara’s mother lay beneath a stone carved with an open window.

At dawn, Mara returned to the southern ridge.

The house was gone.

In its place stood a shallow pond. A brass weather vane rose from the center, its swallow pointing north.

Along the muddy bank, Mara found a folded piece of paper beneath a blue stone.

The rain had not touched it.

She opened the note.

_Mara,_

_If you are reading this, then you found the right moment._

_I wish I had found more of them: more mornings at the kitchen table, more walks home from school, more evenings listening to you explain why clocks lose time. I believed important work was always somewhere far away. I was wrong. The most important hours of my life were the ordinary ones, and I did not recognize them until they were gone._

_Do not wait for me. But if you think of me, think of rain._

_Dad._

Mara sat beside the pond until sunlight broke through the clouds.

In the weeks that followed, Bellweather changed.

Green shoots appeared between the railway ties. The river began moving again, first as a thread, then as a bright, shallow stream. The council removed the strictest water rules. Children built boats from folded paper and raced them along the gutters.

Elias became the stationmaster’s assistant. Records revealed that an Elias Wren had disappeared twenty-three years earlier at the age of fifteen. He was Ada Wren’s great-grandson. At seventy-eight, with only six months of memories between boyhood and old age, he approached each day with astonishment.

Mara continued maintaining the town’s clocks.

But she no longer made them perfect.

A clock in the bakery gained three minutes each week. The school clock lost seven. The mayor’s clock chimed thirteen times at noon, despite repeated complaints. Mara let them wander a little, because she had come to understand that time was not a line of identical boxes.

Some minutes lasted years.

Some years vanished in a breath.

And some moments, ordinary while they were happening, waited quietly inside a person until they were needed.

Whenever rain came, Mara opened the workshop door.

She listened to it tapping on the roof, running from the gutters, gathering in the flowerpots. The cracked barometer still pointed toward STORM, and she never repaired it.

On the first anniversary of the rain, she placed a new clock on the wall. Inside its case, she hid a paper bird and a note addressed to whoever might one day find it.

_When the clock stops, do not be afraid._

_Something may be ending._

_Or something may finally be ready to begin._
